clue.text: Thomas Louis takes account of provenance of duellist

parts.note: Thomas Louis Berger is the American novelist who wrote Little Big Man

explanation.surface: A man named Thomas Louis looks into where a famous swordsman came from.
explanation.walkthrough: The duellist is Cyrano, hero of Rostand's play, who is named after the French town he comes from; 'takes' just joins the novelist's surname to the abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Rostand's swordsman Cyrano takes his title from this town in the Dordogne, so it is his place of origin.

clue.text: "His heart was one of those which most —— us" (Byron)

definitions.text: "His heart was one of those which most —— us" (Byron)

parts.words: "His heart was one of those which most —— us" (Byron)
parts.note: a line from Byron's Don Juan with one verb blanked out; the missing verb means to charm into love

explanation.surface: A line of Byron's verse with a gap for the solver to fill.
explanation.definitionFit: Byron's line about a heart that wins affection uses this verb meaning to make someone fall in love.

clue.text: New lodger, heavily disguised, is Hotspur's ally

indicators.note: a lodger in heavy disguise has had his letters rearranged beyond recognition

explanation.surface: A fresh tenant in heavy disguise turns out to be a rebel's confederate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heavily disguised' rearranges the nine letters of NEW LODGER. Hotspur, in Shakespeare's Henry IV Part 1, rebels alongside the Welsh leader Owain.
explanation.definitionFit: In Henry IV Part 1 the Welsh chieftain Owain joins Hotspur's rebellion against the king, making him a fellow conspirator.

clue.text: Greene heard it at nightfall Simon's state retinue

annotationWithheld.why: Clue as held reads 'Greene heard it at nightfall Simon's state retinue': the last three words are the 5-down clue run in by OCR, so the clue is garbled and no scan is available; the intended clue refers to Graham Greene's novel Rumour at Nightfall.
annotationWithheld.clue: Greene heard it at nightfall Simon's state retinue

clue.text: Simon's state retinue

parts.note: the state is the US state on the Pacific coast, home of Hollywood
a suite is a body of attendants, a retinue

explanation.surface: A playwright's band of followers from one particular American state.
explanation.walkthrough: Neil Simon's 1976 comedy is set in a Beverly Hills hotel, so the whole clue names the play while its pieces give the state and the attendants.
explanation.definitionFit: Neil Simon wrote the comedy of that name, so the playwright's work is literally a state followed by a retinue.

clue.text: His stick was a —— lawyer, weighted with lead" (Conan Doyle)

definitions.text: His stick was a —— lawyer, weighted with lead" (Conan Doyle)

parts.words: His stick was a —— lawyer, weighted with lead" (Conan Doyle)
parts.note: a quotation from Conan Doyle with the gap filled by the Malaysian island that gives its name to a kind of walking cane

explanation.surface: A Sherlock Holmes quotation about a heavy walking stick with one word left out.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'lawyer' of this kind is a cane cut from a palm stem, named after the island off the Malay peninsula; Holmes keeps one in A Study in Scarlet and elsewhere.
explanation.definitionFit: The palm-wood walking stick known as a lawyer is named after this Malaysian island where the palm grows.

clue.text: Music played in Scotland as, quietly, operatic baron supports broken rib

indicators.note: in a down clue the supporting piece sits underneath, so it is written after the other pieces

parts.note: P, for piano, is the musical direction meaning quietly

indicators.note: a broken rib has its letters jumbled into a new order

parts.note: Baron Ochs is the boorish nobleman in Strauss's opera Der Rosenkavalier

explanation.surface: Scottish music is played while an opera singer props up a man with a broken rib.
explanation.walkthrough: 'broken' is the anagram signal for the rib, and 'supports' works because in a down entry the baron's name sits underneath, holding the rest up.
explanation.definitionFit: Pibroch is the classical music of the Highland bagpipe, so these are pieces played in Scotland.

clue.text: Something to do at Ponce de Léon's Bahamian fountain

definitions.text: Something to do at Ponce de Léon's Bahamian fountain

parts.words: Something to do at Ponce de Léon's Bahamian fountain
parts.note: the Spanish explorer sought the Fountain of Youth, said to be on Bimini in the Bahamas; drinking there would stop a person growing old

explanation.surface: A tourist's question about what to do at a famous Caribbean spring.
explanation.definitionFit: Legend says the Fountain of Youth keeps those who drink from it forever young, untouched by the years.

clue.text: Genet rigs new message to all our readers

indicators.note: the letters of the two words are made new by being put in a fresh order

explanation.surface: The French writer Jean Genet arranges a fresh message for the readership.
explanation.walkthrough: 'new' rearranges the nine letters of GENET RIGS; Genet is the French novelist and playwright, here only a source of letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A seasonal salutation addressed to every reader is the sort of message a paper prints at year's end.

clue.text: Hear me inaccurately describe a forbidden place

indicators.note: hearing the words inaccurately garbles them, so their letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone asks to be heard while mislabelling a place that is off limits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'inaccurately' rearranges HEAR ME; this is an older spelling of the women's quarters of a household, and 'describe' only links wordplay to definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The word comes from Arabic haram, forbidden, since the women's quarters were barred to outsiders.

clue.text: Party fringe in Old English is Italian opera based on French novel

definitions.text: Italian opera based on French novel

parts.note: Lab is the short form of the Labour Party

indicators.note: the fringe is placed inside the two letters standing for Old English

parts.note: a hem is the edge or fringe of a garment

explanation.surface: A fringe group in the Old English is linked to a Puccini opera.
explanation.walkthrough: Puccini's opera is based on Murger's Scènes de la vie de bohème; 'in' is the container signal, and the printed 'Part' is an OCR misreading of 'Party'.
explanation.definitionFit: Puccini's 1896 opera adapts Henri Murger's novel of Parisian artists, so it is an Italian work drawn from a French book.

clue.text: The French Lieutenant's Woman

parts.note: the title of John Fowles's novel is read as asking for the name of the woman herself, Sarah

explanation.surface: Simply the title of John Fowles's 1969 novel.
explanation.walkthrough: The title looks like the answer in itself, but the clue wants the surname of Sarah, the heroine the townspeople call the French Lieutenant's Woman.
explanation.definitionFit: Sarah, Fowles's heroine, bears this surname and is the woman of the novel's title.

clue.text: Brightly coloured, like Traherne's wheat

definitions.meaning: an old poetic sense meaning lustrous and shining, as a pearl from the East
Thomas Traherne wrote 'The corn was ... and immortal wheat' in his Centuries of Meditations

explanation.surface: A description of vivid colour, compared with the grain in a mystic's prose.
explanation.definitionFit: The archaic adjective means radiant or lustrous, and Traherne uses it of the shining corn in his Centuries.

clue.text: Mob spotted by poet, classified as 24 ()

definitions.meaning: a mob is a large throng of people
Wordsworth's 'I saw a host of golden daffodils' begins with this word for a throng; daffodils belong to the genus of entry 24

explanation.surface: A rabble seen by a poet and put in the same class as another entry.
explanation.walkthrough: Wordsworth wrote 'When all at once I saw a crowd, / A host, of golden daffodils', and daffodils are narcissi, the answer at 24-across.
explanation.definitionFit: A throng of people is a mob, and Wordsworth's daffodils appeared as a thronging host of flowers.

clue.text: Eloquent style of famous lawyer suggesting endless jail

parts.note: a style is a name or title; the most famous advocate of Rome went by this name

indicators.note: the word for jail loses its final letter, leaving it without an end

parts.note: nick is British slang for a prison

explanation.surface: A speaking manner reminiscent of a great advocate who hints at prison.
explanation.walkthrough: 'endless' cuts NICK, British slang for jail, to NIC; 'suggesting' only links.
explanation.definitionFit: Rome's great orator was a byword for fine speech, so an adjective from his name means rhetorically polished.

clue.text: She possessed the tact required to serve a fiddling addict

definitions.text: She possessed the tact required to serve a fiddling addict

parts.words: She possessed the tact required to serve a fiddling addict
parts.note: the violin-playing, cocaine-taking tenant of 221B Baker Street needed a very patient landlady

explanation.surface: Praise for a woman's diplomacy in looking after a difficult musician with a habit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fiddling' suggests fraud, but Holmes plays the violin and takes cocaine; the landlady who serves him is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Holmes's long-suffering landlady at Baker Street tolerated his violin playing and drug use with remarkable patience.

clue.text: Jamesian character involved in several murders

definitions.text: Jamesian character involved in several murders

parts.words: Jamesian character involved in several murders
parts.note: Jamesian points not to Henry James but to P. D. James, whose poet-detective of Scotland Yard investigates her murder cases

explanation.surface: A figure from a Henry James novel caught up in a string of killings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jamesian' suggests Henry James; the crime writer P. D. James is meant, and her series detective is the commander of Scotland Yard who solves her murders.
explanation.definitionFit: P. D. James's poet-policeman Adam is the detective in fourteen of her murder mysteries.

clue.text: Poet announces court proceedings

indicators.note: an announcement is spoken, so the phrase is heard rather than read

parts.note: a tennis match in progress is tennis on, proceedings on a court

explanation.surface: A poet declares that a lawsuit is under way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'court proceedings' suggests a trial, but the court is a tennis court; 'tennis on' said aloud gives the Victorian Poet Laureate.
explanation.definitionFit: Alfred, Lord Tennyson was the Victorian Poet Laureate who wrote In Memoriam.

clue.text: His templar not knighted but canonized

definitions.text: His templar not knighted but canonized

parts.words: His templar not knighted but canonized
parts.note: the templar is Simon Templar, known as the Saint, so he was made a saint rather than a knight like the medieval Knights Templar

explanation.surface: A remark that a crusading knight was made a saint instead of being knighted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'templar' suggests the Knights Templar; it is Simon Templar, the Saint, hero of Leslie's thrillers.
explanation.definitionFit: Leslie, the thriller writer, created Simon Templar, nicknamed the Saint, the canonized templar of the clue.

clue.text: Whence the "death-light of Africa" rode to the sea

definitions.text: Whence the "death-light of Africa" rode to the sea

parts.words: Whence the "death-light of Africa" rode to the sea
parts.note: Chesterton's poem Lepanto calls Don John the death-light of Africa and has him riding to the sea, naming the land he is from

explanation.surface: A question about where a dreaded African light rode from on its way to the coast.
explanation.walkthrough: In G. K. Chesterton's Lepanto the refrain runs 'Don John of Austria is riding to the sea'; the same poem calls him 'the death-light of Africa'.
explanation.definitionFit: Don John, victor at Lepanto, is styled 'of Austria' as the Habsburg son of Charles V, so that is his homeland.

clue.text: Rapture of Master of the Queen's Musick ()

definitions.meaning: rapture is a state of perfect joy
Sir Arthur held that court post, the senior royal musician, from 1953 until his death in 1975

explanation.surface: The ecstasy of the monarch's chief musician.
explanation.walkthrough: The Master of the Queen's Musick is the official royal composer in Britain; Sir Arthur held the post under Elizabeth II.
explanation.definitionFit: Rapture is perfect happiness, and the composer Sir Arthur of that surname was the monarch's chief musician.

clue.text: Author of bestseller, though few followed In His Steps

definitions.text: Author of bestseller, though few followed In His Steps

parts.words: Author of bestseller, though few followed In His Steps
parts.note: Charles M. ... 1896 novel In His Steps sold millions and asked 'What would Jesus do?', yet few readers lived by it

explanation.surface: A writer whose hit book had few disciples walking in its footsteps.
explanation.walkthrough: 'followed In His Steps' reads as copying the man, but In His Steps is the title of the novel; few readers took up its call to imitate Christ.
explanation.definitionFit: Charles Monroe, the Kansas minister, wrote the hugely popular novel In His Steps, which coined 'What would Jesus do?'.

clue.text: Occurrence of coincidence in the work of Conrad

definitions.meaning: a fortuitous happening, something that comes about by luck
Joseph Conrad's 1913 novel bears this title and was his first commercial success

explanation.surface: Coincidences turn up in a Joseph Conrad novel.
explanation.definitionFit: A coincidence is a happening by luck, and Conrad's 1913 novel of that name was his first popular success.

clue.text: Ski-run accident for art critic

indicators.note: an accident on the slope leaves the letters of the run in a heap in a new order

explanation.surface: A mishap on the ski slope befalls an art critic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'accident' rearranges the letters of SKI-RUN; 'for' only links. John is the Victorian critic of Modern Painters.
explanation.definitionFit: John, the Victorian writer of Modern Painters, was Britain's leading art critic of his age.

clue.text: Beethoven lyricist who brewed Wallenstein's Lager

definitions.meaning: the Ode to Joy in Beethoven's Ninth Symphony sets a poem by Friedrich
Wallensteins Lager, Wallenstein's Camp, is the first play of Friedrich's Wallenstein trilogy; Lager means camp in German

explanation.surface: The man who wrote Beethoven's words also brewed a general's beer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'brewed' makes Lager a beer, but German Lager means camp: Wallensteins Lager is the first part of Friedrich's trilogy.
explanation.definitionFit: Friedrich wrote the Ode to Joy set by Beethoven and the play Wallensteins Lager, the camp of the Thirty Years' War general.

clue.text: Early Elysian bloomers

parts.note: spring flowers of the daffodil family, named for the Greek youth of myth, and in legend growing in the meadows of the Underworld

explanation.surface: Flowers that come up early in the fields of paradise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bloomers' may suggest underwear; it means flowers that bloom, early in spring, and named for the youth of Greek myth.
explanation.definitionFit: Daffodils and their kin are spring bulbs, named after the Greek youth turned into a flower, and pictured in the Elysian meadows.

clue.text: Fabulous swimmers

parts.note: fabulous means belonging to fable, so these are mythical water nymphs who live in rivers and springs

explanation.surface: Praise for some excellent swimmers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fabulous' looks like praise but means from fable or myth: the swimmers are the freshwater nymphs of Greek mythology.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth these nymphs inhabit springs, rivers and lakes, so they are legendary creatures of the water.

clue.text: A hell of a boatman

parts.note: read literally, the boatman belongs to Hell: the ferryman of Greek myth who carries the dead over the Styx

explanation.surface: Admiration for a really impressive sailor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A hell of a' sounds like slang for remarkable; read literally it means the boatman of the Underworld who ferries souls across the Styx.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek ferryman rows the souls of the dead across the river Styx into Hades.

clue.text: Gillian Avery reported his war

parts.note: Gillian Avery's children's novel The ... War tells of the Victorian outcry over Jumbo's sale from London Zoo

explanation.surface: A children's author writes up a man's military campaign.
explanation.walkthrough: 'his war' suggests a soldier, but Gillian Avery's novel The Elephant War concerns the 1882 protest at the sale of Jumbo, London Zoo's star animal.
explanation.definitionFit: Avery's novel is named for the war over Jumbo, the famous London Zoo animal sold to Barnum's circus.
